html:
Atomism is the idea that everything is made of tiny pieces that cannot be cut, moving in empty space. It was first taught in Greece in the 5th century BCE by Leucippus and his pupil Democritus. The word comes from the Greek atomos, "uncuttable".

The atomists were answering the Eleatic philosophers, who argued that change and empty space were impossible. Leucippus and Democritus replied that the void is real and that atoms, endless in number and differing only in shape, size and position, combine and separate to make all the things we see. Nothing is guided by purpose; everything happens by necessity.

Epicurus took up atomism around 300 BCE and built his ethics on it, in what became Epicureanism. The Roman poet Lucretius set it out in On the Nature of Things. Thinkers in India developed their own atom theories separately. Long rejected in favour of Aristotle, atomism came back in the 17th century, and in the early 19th century John Dalton made it the basis of modern chemistry.
